split_method: Strict temporal split: features from 1-14 Oct (weeks 1-2), training target 15-21 Oct (week 3), test on unseen 22-31 Oct. Test cells need 10+ tickets.
preprocessing_summary: Winsorise features and training target at the 1st/99th percentile of TRAIN data, then StandardScaler, both fitted on train rows only inside one Pipeline. Row cap for SVM (12,000) and KNN search (40,000).

classification_models.name: BASELINE tier from weeks 1-2 shrinkage estimate
BASELINE tier from route x hour average

caveats: The 'sparse cell' test only includes cells that later had 10+ tickets (we need a reliable answer to score against). Such cells were BUSIER than they looked in weeks 1-2, which favours any model that can infer 'this place and hour is busy' from location and time. The advantage over the baselines on sparse cells is therefore real but overstated; cells that stay sparse cannot be scored at all.
The fallback is applied with features built from the whole month (not only weeks 1-2), a slightly different window from training.
The target is itself an estimate built from a SAMPLE of riders (mobile e-tickets) scaled by an assumed factor; ML learns to predict that estimate, not a head-count.

concepts.summary: Hide part of the data while the model learns, then score it on the hidden part, so we test understanding and not memory.
concepts.example: A student practises on past papers and is judged on a new paper.

concepts.summary: Train on the past and test on the future, never the other way round, so no future information leaks into training.
concepts.example: Predict next week's bus crowding from the previous three weeks only.

concepts.summary: Rescale every column to a similar range so no column dominates only because its numbers are bigger.
concepts.example: Distance in km and hour of day are put on the same scale before KNN measures 'closeness'.

concepts.summary: Cut extreme values back to the 1st and 99th percentile of the training data so a few huge numbers cannot distort the model.
concepts.example: One day with a ticket-system glitch is capped instead of ruining the average.

concepts.summary: Fits the best straight line (a weighted sum of features) through the data to predict a number.
concepts.example: Predicting house price from size, bedrooms and age.

concepts.summary: Linear regression with a brake: Ridge shrinks all weights, Lasso can shrink some to exactly zero, which also selects features.
concepts.example: A teacher who stops you explaining a result with too many reasons.

concepts.summary: A mix of Ridge and Lasso, useful when several features overlap.
concepts.example: Latitude, longitude and distance to the centre all describe 'where', so their weights are shared sensibly.

concepts.summary: To predict a new case, look at the K most similar known cases and let them vote (or average them).
concepts.example: Judging a restaurant by the ratings of the 10 most similar ones nearby.

concepts.summary: Draws the boundary between classes with the widest possible safety margin; with a kernel the boundary can curve.
concepts.example: Separating spam from normal mail with the cleanest dividing line.

concepts.summary: A flow-chart of yes/no questions that ends in an answer; easy to read but can memorise noise if too deep.
concepts.example: A doctor's triage chart.

concepts.summary: Many different trees vote and their answers are averaged, which is steadier than any single tree.
concepts.example: Asking 200 people to guess the sweets in a jar and taking the average.

concepts.summary: Builds trees one after another, each fixing the mistakes of the previous ones.
concepts.example: A student who redoes only the questions they got wrong, round after round.

concepts.summary: A linear model that outputs the probability of each class instead of a number.
concepts.example: A bank estimating the chance a loan will be repaid.

concepts.summary: Classifies using probabilities and pretends the features are independent, which makes it very fast.
concepts.example: Spam filters multiply the probabilities of the words in a mail.

concepts.summary: With no labels, groups similar items by repeatedly moving K group centres to the middle of their members.
concepts.example: Grouping bus routes into 'morning commuter' and 'all-day' types.

concepts.summary: Squeezes many columns into a few new ones that keep most of the information, so data can be drawn on a 2-D plot.
concepts.example: Plotting routes described by six numbers on a single flat map.

concepts.summary: Repeats the train/test experiment several times on different hidden parts and averages the scores, so one lucky split cannot fool us.
concepts.example: Five mock exams instead of one.

concepts.summary: Tries every combination of a model's settings with cross-validation and keeps the best.
concepts.example: Trying several oven temperatures and times to find the best cake.

concepts.summary: The model memorises the training data and does worse on new data; shown by a big gap between train and test scores.
concepts.example: Learning last year's answers by heart instead of the subject.

concepts.summary: MAE is the average size of the error, RMSE punishes big errors more, R2 is the share of variation explained (1 perfect, 0 no better than the average).
concepts.example: An exam score shows how far off you were on average.

concepts.summary: Accuracy is the share of correct labels; macro-F1 treats every class equally, even rare ones; the confusion matrix shows which classes get mixed up.
concepts.example: A spam filter that is 95% accurate but never catches a rare scam would score poorly on macro-F1.
